speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For Singapore, the good news is that we are living longer, and many of our seniors live fulfilling and active lives, well into their silver years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, ageing also comes with related illnesses and disability.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To enable more of our seniors to age well with dignity and purpose, we need to prepare ahead of time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We need to look at how we can better organise social and health care, how we can enable our seniors to stay healthy, age-in-place and continue to contribute to the community, and how we can support them in their medical and long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have made significant progress in these areas over the past few years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That year, we also developed the Action Plan for Successful Ageing with various stakeholders, which now has over 70 initiatives underway to empower our seniors to live well, even as we live longer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Earlier this year, we announced the Caregiver Support Action Plan to strengthen the support for caregiving for our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include the Home Caregiving Grant, respite care services, and caregiver empowerment and training.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: More recently, we introduced the Merdeka Generation Package, to thank the Merdeka Generation for their contributions to Singapore and provide more support for their healthcare and long-term care needs in their silver years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This follows the Pioneer Generation Package that was introduced in 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One important area we need to address is long-term care financing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In 2016, the ElderShield Review Committee was set up to look into how we can provide greater financial support for Singaporeans who become severely disabled during old age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After rigorous deliberation and extensive public consultation, the Committee submitted its report to the Government last year with the following key recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, higher payouts that increase over time and are for life, so that Singaporeans are better supported for as long as they remain severely disabled; and simpler claim processes, so that severely disabled Singaporeans and their caregivers can apply for claims more conveniently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government accepted the recommendations made by the Committee and the report was debated in Parliament in July last year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We announced our plan to introduce CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The risk-pooling approach through the universal insurance coverage for CareShield Life reflects our desire to nurture an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am glad that it had received support from Members of this House.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Once again, I would like to thank the Committee for their work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Financing our long-term care is a shared responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We come together as a society to pool our risks through insurance, CareShield Life and ElderShield, to address the variability of long-term care costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Individuals and their families also play a part through their own savings, and the Government provides significant support through subsidies and assistance schemes, particularly toward the lower income.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All these three pillars are essential – insurance, savings and Government support – and achieving the right balance among them is crucial in keeping our system inclusive, affordable and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, in addition to strengthening insurance, we have concurrently reviewed how other financing sources of long-term care can complement CareShield Life and ElderShield to better support Singaporeans with disability.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will enhance Government support for long-term care through the establishment of ElderFund in January 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will provide up to $250 per month, especially to those who are unable to join CareShield Life, have low MediSave balances and face financial difficulties in meeting their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is in addition to existing subsidies of up to 80% for long-term care services, such as nursing homes, and various other Government disability assistance schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Around mid-2020, we will also be extending the use of MediSave by allowing Singaporeans to withdraw cash from their own and spouses' MediSave for their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Bill provides the legislative framework for the establishment, governance and administration of the CareShield Life Scheme, and also facilitates the implementation of other long-term care financing measures for the severely disabled I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, clause 5 of the Bill provides for the establishment of the CareShield Life Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It provides for the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board to administer CareShield Life and be responsible for the issuance and servicing of the insurance policies, premium collection, payment of benefits and management of the CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I will talk about the Fund in a short while.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also be appointing the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) as the Administrator.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: AIC will be responsible for the assessment of an individual’s eligibility for the claim by ascertaining his or her disability status.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This division in administrative roles between CPF Board and AIC allows us to tap on the expertise of the respective agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In particular, as AIC administers all of the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) disability schemes, AIC will be the natural touchpoint for seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They are best placed to advise disabled seniors and their caregivers on the various forms of long-term care services and financing schemes they can tap on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill defines the groups of individuals that will be covered under the CareShield Life Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Those who are at least 30 years old will be covered when the Scheme is launched.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Subsequent cohorts would be covered on their birthday when they turn 30 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This provides universal coverage for future generations of Singaporeans, ensuring CareShield Life coverage for them, regardless of their health, pre-existing disability or financial status.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, the Scheme will be optional for older cohorts of Singapore Citizens and PRs born in 1979 or earlier, and they can join the scheme if they do not have pre-existing severe disability.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The ElderShield Review Committee had recommended to keep the scheme optional for them because their circumstances and their needs could vary widely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This makes it more convenient for them to join and they can still choose to opt out before 31 December 2023, if they wish to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, they will be auto-enrolled, but they have the option to opt out of the Scheme and they can do so up to 31 December 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill also provides for CareShield Life to cover all individuals who become Singapore Citizens or PRs after the Scheme commences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These are the new Singapore Citizens and PRs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This way, all new Singapore Citizens and PRs will participate in this national scheme and benefit from better support for their future long-term care needs, just like all Singapore Citizens and PRs today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The only exception is if they are born in 1979 or earlier, the older Singapore Citizens and PR, and are severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Like Singapore Citizens and PRs in those cohorts who are already severely disabled at the launch of CareShield Life, they will also not be able to join the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Part 3 of the Bill provides for Government administration of the ElderShield Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As announced earlier this year, we are transferring the ElderShield scheme, which is currently administered by private insurers, to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will be done in mid-2021, together with the launch of CareShield Life for older Singaporeans born in 1979 or earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The transfer allows ElderShield to be administered on a not-for-profit basis, with CPF Board and AIC as the Government's key administrators.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will facilitate a smooth upgrading from ElderShield to CareShield Life for those who choose to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This Bill will dis-apply the Insurance Act to the transfer, as otherwise the ElderShield portfolios cannot be transferred to the Government because the Government is not included in the definition of "transferee" in the Insurance Act.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, in practice, we will take reference from the requirements the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has put in place in governing the transfer to protect policyholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This includes appointing an independent external auditor to audit the transfer and providing MAS with the full audit reports.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Those who choose not to upgrade to CareShield Life will remain covered by their existing ElderShield policy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, they will also benefit from the improvements to the claim process that will be implemented for CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Now, let me move on to the benefits and payouts of the schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: CareShield Life and ElderShield will remain as basic schemes to benefit severely disabled policyholders, as provided in clause 12 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This keeps premiums affordable, which is crucial for a national scheme like CareShield Life that caters to a broad segment of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Policyholders who prefer higher coverage or better benefits can buy Supplements from private insurers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Existing Supplements administered by the private insurers will not be transferred to the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 16 of the Bill provides for claims to be made for CareShield Life or ElderShield payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We recognise that being severely disabled can be a stressful situation for policyholders and their caregivers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Hence, we want to make the claim process more convenient.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nonetheless, individuals can opt out from the access and disclosure of such disability-related health information, and we will release more details on how individuals can do so nearer the launch date.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But I should point out that if they do so, if they do opt out of the access and disclosure, they will lose some convenience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, severely disabled individuals will not receive any proactive outreach to apply for claims because we do not know their disability status, and they may need to go for a separate disability assessment even if they had been assessed for disability recently at a healthcare institution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, individuals born between 1970 and 1979 will not be auto-enrolled and may need to go for a disability assessment in order to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Part 8 of the Bill also enables CPF Board and AIC to access, subject to certain safeguards, an individual’s confidential information in the possession of another Government department or public authority for the administration of CareShield Life, ElderShield and prescribed social or healthcare-related public schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Again, this is meant to increase convenience for policyholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If convicted, a person may be liable for a fine of up to $5,000, or imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Overall, we want to strike a careful balance between facilitating access and convenience for Singaporeans with the safeguarding of health and confidential information.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This gives claimants the flexibility to decide on their preferred care arrangement, so that they can remain at home or in the community if they wish and still receive the cash payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, it is important that these cash payouts are safeguarded.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will balance between such flexibility and the need for safeguards in several ways.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, some severely disabled policyholders may lack mental capacity and are unable to manage their cash payouts or even apply for claims in the first place.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In this case, a donee or a deputy can act on their behalf to apply for claims and receive and manage the payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the absence of a donee or deputy, clause 16 of the Bill allows certain family members or caregivers to be authorised applicants to make claims on behalf of such policyholders and receive payouts as approved payees so as to support the care of the policyholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, to safeguard against the risk of misuse or fraud, the classes of persons who can make or receive claims will be a tight list approved by the Minister and generally limited to those who are caregivers for the policyholder.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They can only receive the payouts for a limited period of one year, subject to appeals for an extension, if necessary, to give them time to apply to be appointed as a deputy for the policyholder.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, we will allow policyholders or their authorised applicants to nominate healthcare institutions caring for the policyholders, such as nursing homes, as approved payees under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will ensure the continuity of their care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Third, we will require third-party payees to first apply for the payouts for the policyholder’s care, as provided in clause 50 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Not doing so without reasonable excuse is an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If convicted, the penalty is double that for the offence of false declarations or wrongful access of information under clause 48 of the Bill, given that these are offences against vulnerable persons.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This ensures that payouts are prioritised for the care of the policyholder.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Further, we will protect the payouts from creditors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, the Bill allows premium debt to be netted off from the payouts, and we will use this only in the case of willful defaulters who do not pay CareShield Life premiums but have made claims to benefit from the Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will do so in a calibrated manner and will cap the amount of debt netted off from the payouts each month to ensure that policyholders will continue to receive the bulk of the payouts to meet their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The second case is where there are monies owed by the policyholder to a healthcare institution, for instance, a nursing home, arising from the care provided to the policyholder, if the policyholder or authorised applicant has already directed the payouts to this institution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This ensures that healthcare institutions providing care to the policyholder can continue to be adequately resourced to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 14 requires that CareShield Life and ElderShield policyholders pay their premiums in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is so that the schemes will remain solvent and sustainable, and to be fair to other policyholders who have dutifully paid their premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is to encourage early participation in the Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The participation incentives will be netted off their premiums payable over a period of 10 years, thereby reducing the amount of premiums that the policyholders will need to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Policyholders who need further help with their CareShield Life premiums even after premium subsidies and support measures can receive Additional Premium Support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is similar to MediShield Life and is the Government’s commitment to ensure that premiums remain affordable and that no one loses CareShield Life coverage due to his or her inability to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, there may be a small group of willful defaulters who refuse to pay their CareShield Life premiums despite having the means to do so, even after reminders have been sent to them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Any CareShield Life premiums defaulted that cannot be recovered is a burden that will be shouldered by other policyholders in the form of higher premiums eventually.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To be fair to the other policyholders, we need to take a strict stance against these willful defaulters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, Part 7 of the Bill provides for a premium recovery framework that is similar to the approach for MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Penalties and interest can be imposed on outstanding premiums, and we intend to similarly appoint the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore as a recovery body to recover outstanding premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For ElderShield policyholders who do not pay their premiums, their ElderShield cover will lapse after the grace period, similar to their current terms and conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Premiums collected under CareShield Life and ElderShield will flow into the CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund that will be established by clause 35 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The insurance fund will be a self-sustaining fund, supported by the premiums collected under both schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund will be managed by CPF Board in a not-for-profit manner, for the benefit of policyholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Fund moneys can only be used for policyholders’ benefit and scheme administration.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government or CPF Board, as the Fund administrator, cannot remove any Fund moneys for its own use, except for the cost of operating the schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to assure Singaporeans that there are safeguards in place to ensure proper scheme governance for both CareShield Life and ElderShield.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These include safeguards over the scheme parameters and administration, the collection of premiums and payment of claims, and management of information.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, the governance of scheme parameters and administration will be overseen by an independent CareShield Life Council, to be appointed by the Minister under clause 37 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Council will review and make recommendations on policy and scheme parameters, to ensure that the schemes provide protection for Singaporeans in an affordable and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This includes reviewing CareShield Life's premium and payout increases beyond 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For the first five years of CareShield Life's implementation, until 2025, both premiums and payouts will increase at 2% per year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Adjustments thereafter will be reviewed by the Council.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In addition, the Council will review the administration of the schemes and advise on matters related to the investment of the CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Council will be appointed by the time the CareShield Life Scheme takes effect.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will comprise members with various professional expertise and a wide range of experience to perform the key functions of the Council.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are in the midst of setting up the Council, and will share more information later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, the Bill aims to ensure proper collection of premiums and payment of claims to protect the interest of policyholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clauses 48 and 49 of the Bill make false declarations and fraudulent disability assessment offences, with penalties to deter such offences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned earlier, the Bill will also enhance the role of personal and family savings, and Government support in helping the severely disabled with their long-term care costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These measures will help older Singaporeans who are not covered under ElderShield or CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Severely disabled Singapore Citizens and PRs who are at least 30 years old will be able to make cash withdrawals from their own and their spouses’ MediSave Accounts to support their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Clause 66 of the Bill will amend the CPF Act to allow for this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These cash withdrawals will supplement the CareShield Life or ElderShield payouts that they may be receiving.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will enhance the role of personal and family savings in supporting long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Like CareShield Life and ElderShield, similar safeguards will be in place for those who lack mental capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Apart from allowing withdrawals from MediSave for long-term care, the Government will also play a part in helping Singaporeans with their cost of long-term care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Monies in the Fund will be used to fund premium subsidies and participation incentives for the CareShield Life Scheme and to provide financial support for severely disabled persons under prescribed public schemes, such as Elder Fund, which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Long-Term Care Support Fund is in addition to existing Government subsidies for long-term care services, such as nursing homes, home care and centre-based care services, existing Government assistance schemes, as well as the new Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, just to repeat, the support fund holds the Government funding to help the Scheme through premium subsidies and so on, whereas the insurance fund holds the monies from premium payments which is used to fund payouts from the schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Both Funds will be accounted for and managed separately and the accounts of each Fund will be made public.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our society is ageing and we need to prepare for this ahead of time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: CareShield Life is a major step in expanding the role of insurance in the long-term care financing landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Bill goes beyond long-term care insurance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Bill also enables enhancements to be made to the other two pillars of our long-term care financing system through the withdrawal of MediSave for long-term care and ElderFund.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With the strengthening of the roles of insurance, savings and Government assistance, Singaporeans can have better protection and greater assurance for their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This way, Singaporeans can live long and with greater peace of mind.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also reassured by some of the additional provisions in this Bill, such as ElderFund, which seek to strengthen the framework of long-term care in Singapore, because although CareShield Life aims for universal coverage, there are necessarily some situations where it is not scoped to address.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But now that we are here at the business end of things, I have several clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And how will the Government support older Singaporeans who are unable or unwilling to enrol in CareShield Life, should they become significantly disabled in the future?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, how can disbursements from the soon to be established ElderFund be calibrated to support these disabled seniors and will payouts from ElderFund be also adjusted according to medical and cost of living inflation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To quote from the GPC's recommendations on CareShield Life, we noted that, and I quote, "a careful balance has to be struck between increasing and expanding benefits so that the programme remains relevant and useful, and yet keeping the scheme both affordable and sustainable for the long term.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If ElderShield is to be universal with mandatory enrollment, then the GPC believes that the Government will have to provide targeted financial assistance to ensure that all Singaporeans will be able to participate in this social security programme, which is designed to increase peace of mind in the event of severe disability." Hence, I would appreciate clarifications from the Ministry as to how it intends to maintain premium affordability for CareShield Life, while ensuring that Singaporeans are suitably buffered against rising long-term care costs, particularly when they are only either mildly or moderately disabled and thus requiring financial support?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that the Minister just mentioned that the criteria would be the same as for MediShield Life Additional Premium Support.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But my question is: should the criteria be the same, given the fact that the operational circumstances for CareShield Life and MediShield Life are fundamentally different?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The GPC also supports that Supplemental Plans from Private Insurers continue to be offered for CareShield Life and I am glad that a mechanism is built to provide for that, as it was the case for ElderShield.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will certainly grant flexibility and meet the needs of Singaporeans who feel that they would be willing to purchase additional coverage.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry be able to comment whether private insurers will, indeed, be prepared to provide such Supplements for additional coverage for CareShield Life, and whether Singaporeans will be able to use their MediSave to purchase or to cover such additional coverage?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask if the Ministry is aware if any of the private insurers is currently planning to introduce a Supplement whereby perhaps payouts can be activated at a lower threshold, specifically when a policyholder has two instead of three affected activities of daily living (ADLs).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This was the feedback that has come up here and there, and there were questions on why three instead of two ADLs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The GPC actually felt that there could be scope for private insurers to meet these gaps.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if not, what are the reasons that this is not being considered by the private insurers?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There has been some feedback in the past about the claims process for ElderShield, that the pool of disability evaluators was limited and the process of evaluation and re-evaluation was both onerous and unwieldy.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, there was feedback that for claimants, the requirements for re-evaluation could be too frequent.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I would appreciate clarifications regarding how the claims process for CareShield has, indeed, been streamlined, while at the same time I would also like to know how we can guard against fraudulent claims and ensure that the payouts actually reach their intended targets.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed introduction of a National Electronic Health Records system and, of course, the recent incidents of data leaks and hacks, notably the hacking of SingHealth's information technology (IT) system have thrown the issue of data integrity and security into sharp focus.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I would like to ask how would the administrators of CareShield Life safeguard policyholder data that is being collected and also that is being used for the purposes of the scheme?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thus, we had urged that the quantum of payouts be reviewed at fixed intervals and revised according to a formula that takes into account both general consumer and medical inflation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We had further proposed that there be a framework for periodic review of the premiums to ensure that the scheme remains both sustainable and affordable.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Minister has touched briefly on how this would be done.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would like to understand a little bit better as to exactly how and how often the Ministry intends to review and adjust payouts and premiums.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I view the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Bill as the finishing piece of an encompassing "medical safety net" that includes the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS), MediShield Life and MediFund.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill has its good points but also some minus points in several areas which I shall elaborate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I shall start with this Bill’s plus points.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One, the lifetime payout is welcome as severely disabled individuals require lifelong assistance with their daily living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, the setting up of the Long-Term Care Support Fund which sets aside monies for premium subsidies and incentives, capital injection and other public schemes that provide support for disabled persons.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This fund will ensure that the CareShield Life premiums will be affordable for the majority.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, those eligible severely handicapped presently will receive CareShield Life payouts immediately for life after paying their first premium.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is rightly so that we can show benevolence to this group of Singaporeans with this immediate payout.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I consider the following as minus points for this Bill.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While I can understand that higher payouts will require higher premiums, the purpose of insurance is to give peace of mind on future unforeseen needs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In view of its inadequacy, there is a need to depend on personal savings or family help should the need arise.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For better piece of mind and coverage, individuals can take up extra insurance for higher payouts with private insurers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: On MediSave withdrawals for Long-Term Care of $200 per month for the severely disabled who are above 30 years old and subject to a minimum MediSave balance of $5,000, can they tap on their children’s or siblings’ MediSave once their own MediSave has been exhausted?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For Pioneers, can they also receive this assistance on top of the $100 per month PG Disability Assistance Scheme and the use of MediSave of $200 per month?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the criteria be made less stringent, for example, with two ADLs instead of three ADLs to qualify?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, the "three ADLs" criterion for CareShield Life eligibility claim is challenging.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While I agree that there will be a lot more claimants with two ADLs instead of three ADLs, thus resulting in higher premiums, my contention is that many, if not all, afflicted with two ADLs cannot continue to work as before.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They would need to depend on personal savings or family members.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, better awareness on long-term care financing and long-term care insurance should be raised so that people can better plan ahead for possible eventualities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Three, claimants of CareShield Life payouts must go through the stringent assessment by stipulated assessors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Minister exempt those newly discharged from hospitals from assessment by stipulated assessors once specified by their own public hospital doctors to be having three ADLs?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can public doctors looking after their own patients endorse the three ADLs, since they know their patients well?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Minister consider setting up a one-stop assistance channel or centre for mobility-afflicted Singaporeans to tap on the various available schemes?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, patients on discharge from hospitals can be assisted to claim for Home Caregiving Grant, MediSave withdrawal, Elderfund, Pioneer Generation Disability Scheme, Senior Mobility Fund, Interim Disability Assistance Programme for the Elderly (IDAPE) and so on?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The reason is that many Singaporeans do not know the various schemes available or how to apply for them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially useful and convenient for those low-income patients who are already applying for MediFund to pay for their hospital bills.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They have already given all the eligibility information to hospitals for MediFund assistance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Minister make it easier for relevant Ministries to share information, so that claimants do not need to submit the same documents multiple times for various subsidies?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors with three ADLs living in the community will also benefit from the one-stop assistance channel for referrals to various Ministries to claim insurance or to apply for subsidies.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Minister assist in identifying and facilitating this group of Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Home care is an important component of Long-Term Care services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a good alternative to institutional care setting for many reasons.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: But our home care in Singapore is presently inadequate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is worrying, with our fast-ageing population and the fast increasing need for home care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Minister expand home care quickly with the tenets of prevention of further deterioration of physical frailty and mental disorder, such as depression?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Ageing Gracefully at Home programme at Chin Swee, supported by AIC, is a good home care programme.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This home care provides the seniors living alone in HDB rental flats with medical, social and daily needs, nursing care, mental wellness and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will facilitate many Singaporeans to age gracefully with their loved ones in the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In a small family environment, the burden of care for the elderly would fall squarely on one or two members of the household.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For a family with no children, such burden would exacerbate rapidly when the couple grows old and neither one of them is able to care for one or the other.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At our Meet-the-People Sessions, we would have heard stories of the struggles and challenges faced by our residents in looking after the elderly, while trying to raise a family of their own and having to make ends meet all at the same time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We heard in this Chamber last year that this Government intends to focus on building an inclusive society where no Singaporean, young or old, healthy or sick, gets left behind.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Bill is a step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the debate on the Motion on ElderShield and CareShield Life in the middle of 2018, the Workers' Party Members spoke in support of the rationale to strengthen our social safety net for the long-term care needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: CareShield Life, as the Minister had stated then, would be a basic protection scheme for Singaporeans against severe disability during their old age and the scheme would be inclusive, affordable and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And what about Singaporeans who are unable to do one or two out of three ADLs currently?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would they be able to enrol into CareShield Life or be assisted by ElderFund only, as highlighted by the Minister earlier?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, on the point of affordability, I would like to ask the Minister to share with the House on the impact of the introduction of CareShield Life on the adequacy of the MediSave accounts for future cohorts of Singaporeans who would be enrolled into the compulsory scheme upon attaining the age of 30.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Take the case of a young father who is servicing the MediShield Life premiums for his children and himself, and perhaps even his spouse, using his MediSave account.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would this person have enough in his MediSave account to pay for CareShield Life as well or when the transitional subsidies for the scheme expires?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The affordability of CareShield Life needs to be considered in context with MediShield Life, since both schemes are made compulsory for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is there any impact study done on the adequacy of the MediSave accounts of our young working class Singaporeans with the introduction of such mandatory insurance schemes?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: On the same issue of affordability, may I ask the Minister again, are the premium calculations for CareShield Life heavily influenced by the MOH estimates that one in two Singaporeans aged 65 and above could become severely disabled in their lifetime?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If we were to strip away the international data from the MOH estimates, how would the percentage look like?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Senior Minister of State had mentioned some of these factors in passing in his speech on the subject last year.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Factors, such as the disability mortality rate, recovery rate, disability incidence and risk profile for various cohorts, to name a few, are important information for the public, not just to determine whether Singaporeans are being charged baseline premiums or way above it, but to spur them to make informed choices to live healthily.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: What is the projected savings from this exercise and did the Ministry work these savings into the premium calculations?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And what would be the projected profit and loss for the CareShield Life scheme under the sole administration of CPF Board, assisted by AIC?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although this is a not-for-profit insurance scheme, it does not mean that there is no profit generated.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am sure the Ministry would have crunched the numbers in the run-up to the introduction of CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is in the public interest that the Ministry should release such information.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am also sure that the Ministry can easily illustrate the technical details of the actuarial model for CareShield Life in simple graphics or something easy for the general public to digest.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Sustainable long-term care requires the following three elements: first, financing; second, delivery and this is where we need the three "Cs" – capacity, capability and coordination; and thirdly, regulation of some form.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In many countries today, the distribution of care is shared among the public, private and people sectors.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, co-sharing is among the Government, the individual and the family, and it is a model that we are quite used to.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Essentially, the following four modes of funding are utilised for healthcare: (a) Government subsidies in different forms; (b) MediSave; (c) Basic healthcare insurance, which is our MediShield Life; and (d) MediFund for those who really cannot afford and have no other sources of assistance.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For long-term care, ElderShield is the scheme and now, with migration to CareShield.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The demands for long-term care will increase significantly with the ageing population, the coming of age of our Baby Boomers and, of course, the population and others who may develop complications of chronic illnesses which we have a lot of.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Financing will always put a high demand on governments on various platforms.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In this aspect, I have a few queries and clarifications pertaining to the Bill.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister explain on the decision and rationale for the cut-off at 30 years?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is because, with ElderShield, we earlier saw that it started at 40.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is a difference of 10 years, and it would be useful for us to understand the difference of 10 years and why we are starting a lot earlier with CareShield Life.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: From a medical perspective, I can certainly understand that.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But maybe from a financial perspective and an administrative perspective, we can get a better understanding of this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What type of processes do they have to go through?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister also outline the steps and requirements for those who are alone and in nursing homes and for those with no next-of-kin support?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Pertaining to the disability assessment, on what grounds can the assessment fees be waived?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are there steps or application forms that the applicants will have to pay for such waiver?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Please also review the process and make sure that it is simple enough because many of them can be illiterate or they may not be able to understand what is being asked.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: On the same matter of assessment, some of these people with disability are still in the process of review.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That means that disability has not reached a stable stage and they will need regular review in our healthcare institutions to make sure that it is not progressing further.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Minister did mention that we can have data obtained from our healthcare institutions for those people who need regular reviews.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But then again, is this sufficient or would they have to pay every time they need to have an assessment done by one of the appointed assessors?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, that part is something that most elderly people, those with disability and members who have a disabled person in their families are concerned about.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can these also be tapped on because I think most family members would want to support the disabled member in their family?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can I also ask the Minister on what are our plans moving forward for long-term care at home?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We can do so much more in this area, which is an option besides institutionalisation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What kind of further support at home, in terms of training, respite for caregivers at home who need a break from the caregiving process, are we able to assist families with?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, on the issue of capacity, even in the step-down care area, whether it is at home or in institutions, how are we planning to cope with the supply of manpower?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Today alone, we are highly dependent on foreign nursing and caregiving workforce in this area.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, how sustainable is this and what are the supplementation and injections we are planning, moving forward?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We know that for people who have very severe psychological or psychiatric problems, they may not even be able to perform their ADLs.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, perhaps there is also a need to review and align this with the Ministry of Social and Family Development and other Ministries and see how we can assist these families as well, because the number of people with psychological disability and severe forms of psychological and psychiatric disabilities are increasing and bound to increase further.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There has been some issues raised about the number of ADLs that we can actually include under our consideration for certain schemes, whether it is one, two, three or four.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   In 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) stated that long-term quality care is related to two factors; first, the type of care provided and, second, the lack of integration among different healthcare services.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Minister whether we can focus on these aspects in the forward planning for this sector because this sector is a very important one.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, even more messages, educational information and advertisements are needed.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, we had to conduct more dialogue sessions and discussions, such as case studies, where we can show our families, especially those from the low-income groups, how to obtain assistance from the good schemes made available by our Ministry.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: When a friend of mine turned 40, she received a letter informing about the ElderShield scheme.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: She shared some thoughts that crossed her mind when she first saw the letter.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I can imagine what many at that age would be thinking as they read the collaterals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Why the need for such a scheme at this age?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They are healthy, have an active income and ageing is certainly a distant concept for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But what many fail to think of is that health issues can take many forms and impact anyone regardless of age, in particular, when one suffers disabilities as a result of illness or become mentally incapacitated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The real challenge is what happens if one is not financially prepared or does not have the means to take care of themselves in the long term?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This burden inevitably falls on the family and not on themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One can be physically normal, not disabled, but simply fails to get about their daily activities once dementia sets in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I came across a resident who, unfortunately, suffered dementia at the age of 52.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Fifty-two years old, in today's context, is not old age, especially not so, given the longer life expectancy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, this resident who had dementia will have to depend on another person to manage his daily activities for the rest of his life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Having to care for him not only raises concerns about the cost of care in the long run, but also who in the family would become the primary caregiver from then on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In other encounters with people who needed long-term care, it is those children or youths who are born with physical disabilities or lack the mental capacity to care for themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Parents that I met with children of special needs are genuinely concerned.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The parents are worried that if they themselves grow older, physically and financially taking care of their children will become a significant task.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is a worry they grapple with constantly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While the Bill provides details around the implementation and governance of the funds in the interest of the beneficiaries, I wish to raise a few areas for consideration and some questions for further clarification.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Whilst the financial aspect of their caregiving may be taken care of through CareShield Life, but if they do not have an LPA in place, in the event that they become unable to make decisions for themselves, there presents a risk that their family members will have to fork out additional legal fees to act on their behalf.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While clause 16 provides an option for the family members to act on their behalf if a donee or a deputy is not in place, but would it not be better if they have an LPA from the onset of joining the scheme?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This would mean a less likely potential lapse in their coverage if the family is unable to afford the legal fees.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, under clause 6(b), it specifies that for all Singaporeans and PRs born before 1980 who are not severely disabled before becoming citizens or PRs will automatically qualify for CareShield Life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This group of individuals in Singapore are not the bulk of the population.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, a universal insurance coverage of this nature will form a necessary and central support for them and, financially, it is more manageable for their families.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Earlier in the speech, the Minister just mentioned about the Long-term Care Fund that will provide them the access to their own MediSave or that of their spouses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But we should also be cognisant that these individuals may be unlikely to have worked by that age, or they might not even have sufficient funds in their CPF to have this coverage and may not even have a spouse or a spouse who have that fund to help them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, when a compulsory insurance scheme is implemented, it is understandable for low-income families to be anxious about whether they can reasonably afford the annual premiums.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Fourth, for schemes that look into the long-term needs of individuals, it is judicious for a strong governance process to be established.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This Bill addresses several aspects and clause 50 seeks to focus on preventing the misuse of funds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, clause 20 does indemnify the healthcare institutions or service providers by those with disabilities, wherein they can have access to their patients' funds after providing the service.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On this note, I hope more clarity can be offered if any audit process will be instituted to verify the sums charged by the healthcare institutions or service providers are within the affordable range.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Also, that their services rendered are duly monitored to ensure the vulnerable is receiving proper care, especially if the vulnerable does not have a next-of-kin.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Fifth, when the need arises for an assessment of an individual's condition of disabilities, it is stated that the charges will be based on per type of disability assessed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is pertinent that we implement the schemes well and provide reprieve for families who may face untimely and unfortunate health conditions in any of their family members.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I look forward to more details on the scheme and clarifications on the points raised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill also amends the CPF Act to make provisions for CPF withdrawals for long-term care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The insurers will transfer to the Government the liabilities and corresponding assets backing these liabilities for all policies under the ElderShield scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Worker's Party Members debated most of these provisions in the House last year and supported the general move towards risk-pooling for financing elder disability while raising a number of questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall make a number of points at this stage to reiterate the views we had expressed earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This kind of transparency will ensure greater public buy-in by providing some assurance that premiums have not been set at too high a level that will tend to over-reserve funds that may either need to be disbursed by way of future premium rebates or which may be retained for the benefit of future cohorts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such transparency will also pre-empt the spread of misinformation and ill-informed speculation about the CareShield Life scheme, as Member Mr Pritam Singh argued last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, will transparent policy guidelines be given to the CareShield Life Council to determine the extent to which excess funds, if any, are to be disbursed via premium rebates as opposed to reserving those funds for future cohorts so that the system can be seen to be inter-generationally fair?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Premium rebates are considered once every five years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CareShield's acceptance would benefit from similarly transparent guidelines binding on the CareShield Life Council rather than the Council simply having discretion to make such decision and inform the public after the fact.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourthly, will the Government consider reducing the onerous three ADLs test to two ADLs test using the Long-term Care Fund to administer premium subsidies to defray and defer increment hikes that may be necessitated by this change?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, moving on from points made in the 2018 debate in this House, I would like to raise several new points and questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Government envisage that a competitive CareShield LIfe supplement scheme market will emerge providing competitive premiums and supplements in exchange for higher or less onerously determined payouts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, if so, are there any steps being taken to facilitate this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just to clarify the mechanism for this, does this mean that if the state has provided the grant to reduce the premium and future premium rebate is given to that CareShield Life policyholder, the grant plus interest will be deducted from the premium rebate and returned to the Long-term Care Fund?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, because the changes to this Bill concretise the optimum effects of our ageing society, we should work towards the creation of a vibrant ecosystem that supports many different pathways for the rising number of Singaporeans embarking on their ageing journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the past, the mantra for ageing was that the family members should take care of their elderly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But with our demographic pyramid looking the way it does now, where the ratio of younger people supporting elderly people in more or less every family is much lower than it was, say, 30 years ago, it is no longer possible to view the question of an ageing society solely through the prism of family responsibility alone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What would such a vibrant ecosystem look like?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should, of course, include employment for those who want to continue to work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This group has the right to employment opportunities unscarred by the stigma of ageism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And it should include social support for high levels of activity and social engagement for all older Singaporeans, whether working or not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ecosystem we strive for should include strong capacity for institutionalised care in nursing homes and step-down care facilities to provide care at harmonised and high levels of quality, not to mention elder-friendly facilities in existing and new HDB flats where some progress has been made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should include pathways for ageing-in-place – home care and day care should be widely available geographically, with a variety of providers offering an environment that is competitive and rich in variety and experimentation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifthly, it should include options for assisted living.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Facilities which allow a high degree of autonomy for residents, with shared activity programmes, round-the-clock medical support available on demand, and proximate mixed facilities catering to various age groups so that older Singaporeans do not feel cut off.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does assisted living differ from nursing homes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Please allow me to quote a short passage from Atul Gawande's moving book "Being Mortal", where he talked about one of the founders of assisted living Keren Brown Wilson in the United States (US) state of Oregon in 1980 in a concept she championed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I quote, "The services were, in most ways, identical to the services that nursing homes provide, but here the care-providers understood they were entering someone else's home and that changed the power relations fundamentally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Her philosophy was to provide a place where residents retained their autonomy and privacy of people living in their own homes, including the right to refuse strictures imposed for reasons of safety or institutional convenience." For all pathways, financial assistance should be available that is means-tested and also automatically inflation-indexed based on inflation trends and fiscal resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Facilities catering to a range of budget should be nurtured.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Korean Silver Town model, which I have spoken about in this House, includes a range of facilities, offering different prices and the different degrees of government support from government-run facilities to purely private profit-driven facilities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The facilities in such an ecosystem should be provided by companies, not-for-profit voluntary welfare organisations and, where necessary, government agencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not all eldercare services should be provided by or paid for by the government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where fiscal cost is required, it should be seen in the context of not providing such assistance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It could lead to elderly people living alone becoming cut off and gaining access to medical services only when it is too late when catastrophic conditions set in, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this could have amounted to a far greater drain on the state's coffers downstream in terms of hospital subsidies, MediShield Life premium subsidies, MediFund disbursements and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cost of providing financial assistance should also be seen in the context of the opportunity cost of not providing it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If older Singaporeans lack help to age with purpose and dignity, we could lose out in the vital role of elderly Singaporeans as contributors to the workforce and to the economy as employees, entrepreneurs and customers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not forget the significance of older Singaporeans as role models, mentors, counsellors and caregivers, even when not working.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When elderly Singaporeans cannot afford to leave the house because he or she cannot afford a mobility device, for example, he may be unable to work, he may be unable to be a customer for a neighbourhood business, he may be unable to help his family.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we move towards a future where one in four Singaporeans will be aged over 65, let us strive for successful ageing, both for older Singaporeans and those of us not yet old.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said this, I have a few questions and suggestions regarding our whole-of-society approach towards successful ageing that is of indirect but nevertheless unmistakable relevance to the concerns that underlie this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems that other countries are far ahead of Singapore in this respect as the concept dates back to the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In advanced countries like Finland and Japan, assisted living facilities (ALFs) are growing faster than nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would urge the Government to accelerate the launch of new sites.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Assisted living, at its best – and to be sure, not all existing ALFs in the world represent that best by any means – but at its best, assisted living promises to marry autonomy with good quality medical care and social connectedness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It could be a key pillar for successful ageing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In building this pillar, we have the opportunity to work with local enterprises and startups to develop know-how in operating ALFs in the Southeast Asian cultural context, know-how that could be exported to the region in future, where ageing is a major challenge in countries like Thailand and Malaysia, to the benefit of our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, productivity is a key challenge for this traditionally labour-intensive sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Social robotics, wearable technology and other innovations are being used in the eldercare sector globally, including in some countries in the region like Japan, Korea and China.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What efforts are being made by the Government and non-governmental players to study these innovations and aim to bring them to Singapore by way of engagement with companies and not-for-profits, both at home and abroad?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We all want a health system that is low-cost, grants timely access to all who need care and ensures that healthcare is of high quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But all three at once is impossible to achieve, so we need to choose between difficult tradeoffs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have, by international standards, solved the health system problem better than most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In 2000, WHO ranked Singapore sixth in the world in overall health system performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because this ranking was so controversial – the US ranked 37th behind all the Western European countries – the WHO has never updated the ranking since.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But if you look at more up-to-date figures, we are doing well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Bill will create a universal, prefunded long-term care insurance plan, at least for younger cohorts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because CareShield Life is universal and will be supported by subsidies for low-income Singaporeans, I believe this will provide genuinely universal access to long-term care if we become severely disabled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A mandatory universal plan is particularly important because the likelihood that we will become severely disabled is quite high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, CareShield is not really an insurance scheme in the sense of protecting Singaporeans against a low risk, high-cost event.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is really a prefunding scheme for care needs that are part and parcel of old age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The mandatory nature of CareShield Life will ensure that no Singaporean or their families will be in desperate want of financial assistance to cope with care needs in old age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Cost effectiveness and quality will also be important, but they will have to be addressed another day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to examine how we propose to use the MediSave system to prefund CareShield Life and what the implications are for our broader healthcare financing system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is ironic, given our excellent health outcomes and our comprehensive medical financing system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our top healthy life expectancy ranking worldwide is surely not a sign of a people who cannot afford quality healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it is not so difficult to understand once we appreciate that a fundamental policy lever we have used to manage the cost, access and quality tradeoff is to emphasise individual responsibility whenever possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It appears Singaporeans have internalised this policy principle of individual responsibility quite well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And individual responsibility has been made practical through our MediSave medical savings scheme which gives Singaporeans a nest-egg to spend on their future medical needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong, then Second Minister for Health, said in the debate on the MediSave Scheme in 1983, and I quote: “We must, therefore, save when we can, put a few dollars aside every month when we are working, save as an individual, save as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is the basic idea of MediSave – to provide funds for our citizens to pay for their future health needs, for them to buy an umbrella when it rains; and even before it rains.” But MediSave has a policy objective that extends beyond prefunding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the policy problem was only prefunding for future healthcare costs alone, it would not matter whether MediSave was collected as individual accounts or whether the Government created an endowment fund for future healthcare spending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The policy objective of MediSave was also to encourage efficiency in healthcare utilisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: MediSave achieved this by giving each Singaporean an individual financial stake in their healthcare decision-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew, in the book, "Lee Kuan Yew: Hard Truths to Keep Singapore Going", said of MediSave, "My major objective in the early days was to make sure that nobody derails the idea of having individual accounts for CPF and MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is yours and if you don't use it, you can leave it to your children or relatives or whoever you like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Why should you put it into a common pool and everybody draws out at your expense, which is what is happening in some Western countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The system has collapsed." As in many other matters, Mr Lee was prescient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I suspect many Members dealing with appeals from constituents feel that the problem with individual accounts is holding the line against requests to use MediSave for all types of personal medical and other expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since 1983, there have been dozens of Parliamentary Questions and "cuts" that appeal for the use of MediSave to be extended to many non-hospitalisation healthcare expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when Mdm President was a Member in this House, she filed cuts in the Budget 2006 debate to call for greater flexibility in the use of MediSave, particularly for long-term chronic illnesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has generally held the line, although MediSave's scope has generally been expanded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In isolation, I think holding firm to the policy is admirable, provided that Singaporeans who appeal to access their MediSave funds are given other means of financial assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But if you were to read Mr Lee’s statement on MediSave carefully, you will see that the other problem with individual accounts is holding the line against the Government itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The risk is that policymakers will appropriate the funds in MediSave to finance healthcare expenditures on a universal basis, or indeed, meet any other healthcare expenditure needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the same discipline that the population is expected to exercise in using MediSave wisely must also apply to the policymaker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The policymaker has tended increasingly to see the MediSave account as a convenient source of healthcare financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is enough to fund the operating expenses of MOH for about 10 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What will be the impact of CareShield Life on our MediSave system?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
