text: If you take this as a lump sum premium, this would amount to nearly half of the aggregate MediSave balances currently existing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, the plan is for CareShield Life to be funded over the decades, through premium payments amounting to a few percentage points of a member's monthly MediSave contribution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the total amount collected under CareShield Life – and paid out – will be staggering over the next few decades, just as the sums collected and paid out for MediShield Life have been.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem I have outlined goes beyond just the creation of schemes, such as MediShield Life and CareShield Life, which have greatly improved access to healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The MediSave account has become a source of funds that the policymaker can use to adjust the balance of subsidies in healthcare financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As average balances in MediSave increase, it will become more feasible to propose higher basic rates of coverage in MediShield Life, and in CareShield Life, with the accompanying higher premiums.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hospitalisation and long-term care subsidies as well can be adjusted if MediSave balances are robust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But of course, this subsidy level could fall in the future if CareShield Life payouts became more generous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think there is nothing sinister in this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is just a matter of whether payment is taken through the MediSave pocket or the taxpayers' pocket.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we may come to a point where we can reasonably ask if the individual ownership of the MediSave account remains a meaningful policy principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I respect this principle tremendously, but as we adapt our healthcare policies to address the challenges of an ageing society, we should take a hard look at some of the ideological principles behind healthcare financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I would urge that we examine carefully our assumption that individual responsibility through paying from MediSave and cash, actually reduces moral hazard – the excessive consumption of healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As a matter of health economics, this is an empirical and not a theoretical question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is true in theory that when healthcare coverage is provided free at the point of treatment, there will be increased demand and over-consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the extent and magnitude of these effects are not settled, and the policy question is often too narrowly framed as one of medical cost management only.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: An array of studies from healthcare insurance coverage experiments in the US suggests that other social outcomes matter as well, such as financial and psychological stress, and early detection and management of chronic diseases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I would urge that we also recognise that the MediSave account must be protected from the policymaker, just as it must be protected from the account owner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The issue, I think, is not the misuse or abuse of MediSave funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am quite sure that this Government poses no such risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The issue, rather, is the use of MediSave to alter how healthcare financing is structured without a full and frank examination of how we should be balancing payments between prefunding and current payments, between the individual and the taxpayer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should not let this policy decision pass unexamined.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the recent years, I noted that both MOH and CPF have allowed more flexibility on the withdrawal of CPF funds to assist with the care needs of the elderly or disabled as well as provide additional assistance for their maintenance.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I applaud the move to allow cash withdrawals of up to $200 per month from MediSave accounts to pay for expenses for the severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This allows greater flexibility for those who may have informal care arrangements.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: CPF members can also apply to withdraw their CPF savings on medical grounds.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to acknowledge the designation of AIC as a one-stop agency to assist families on matters relating to our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The work of AIC is wide and diverse and often very difficult.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These include coordinating the work of the Silver Generation Office, to assigning subsidised nursing home vacancies and assessing the need for motorised wheelchairs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While CareShield Life addresses this problem going forward, as Singapore Citizens and PRs born in 1980 or later automatically join this scheme in 2020, most of the elderly today are not even enrolled in ElderShield and thus have very little financial support when it comes to their long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, I hope MOH can do more to help this group.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this is unlikely to be sufficient for the hiring of an FDW or to put an elderly in a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the past few years, we have seen the introduction of the Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation packages which are cohort-based and not means-tested.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is my suggestion that if the Government should have sufficient fiscal surpluses in future, it should move away from cohort-based packages, to set up a long-term care package which will provide low- to middle-income families with additional assistance to take care of their elderly.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When our loved ones are cared for well, we enjoy the peace of mind to contribute productively to the economy and country.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, this Bill must not leave out or undervalue significant groups of people as that would go against its policy intent of being universal and inclusive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Besides urging for a critical change in how we define disability as I have in the past, I would also like to highlight the need to better support our younger Singaporeans who may have disabilities or are in need of long-term care, and also how the current policies discriminate against women.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill can and must go further to strengthen our social fabric and safety nets so that we truly walk the talk of being an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend the ElderShield Review Committee in recommending that the impact of cognitive impairments on functional ability be explicitly considered in the disability assessment framework for claims, and am glad that MOH has accepted this recommendation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These are numbers specifically for this age group and only counts Singaporeans who suffer from minor mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: According to the Institute of Mental Health's latest nationwide study, "One in seven people in Singapore has experienced a mental disorder in their lifetime".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the number of Singaporeans who will be affected, there is an urgent need to examine how long-term care costs for people with mental health conditions are supported.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While people with mental health conditions may be able to perform the physical ADLs, our current policies fail to recognise that they may struggle with other ADLs which are just as essential to everyday life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These may include cognitive ADLs like communication or simple problem-solving, aspects which are not recognised within our current definition but are captured in internationally-recognised assessment tools like the Functional Independence Measure Instrument.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, there is already precedence in our public policy which considers the impact of mental health conditions on daily living, like how the intake assessment for nursing home residents includes aspects of psychiatric conditions, thereby recognising that people with mental health conditions may require support as much as those who have physical disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, urge the Government to take a more inclusive approach in the definition of disabilities, both nationally and in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To be inclusive, we should ensure our policies and schemes provide coverage and support for long-term care for people with mental health conditions, and we can start doing so with CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We should consider how specific mental health conditions that are highly prevalent are recognised and supported by other long-term care schemes, eventually moving to a more universal and explicit recognition of all mental health conditions in our long-term care policies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A critical start could be in how we explicitly consider mental health conditions when defining and assessing disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, we can include assessment of equally critical but non-physical ADLs like cognitive ADLs in functional assessments, or as doctors have advocated for regarding disability assessments, assess and score what patient actually does rather than what patients can do.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This important differentiation between capacity and performance is crucial because it is what we do which actually determines care needs and, hence, caregiver burden.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, an elderly who lives alone in a rental flat – I will call him Marcus.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He is terminally ill and unable to perform two physical ADLs, on top of his mental health condition which affects his cognitive ADLs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Despite his condition, Marcus will not be eligible for this network of schemes designed to support people like him.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of enjoying support, Marcus had to agonise over the financial difficulties, which creates stress and anxiety which adds to his mental health condition.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For both Marcus, who is already suffering from multiple conditions, and his caregiver, their journey in seeking care and support in his last days was unnecessarily difficult.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When we adopt such an extreme definition of severe disability, we inevitably exclude and prevent support from reaching those with more moderate or milder forms of disabilities who are inadequately covered in terms of financial support.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is 35% more than what the average household in Singapore spends on similar items, according to data from the 2017/2018 Household Expenditure Survey.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned how this may affect retirement adequacy of family caregivers, or foster inter-generational transfers of long-term care costs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To prevent the cliff effect created when many schemes concentrate on severe disability as the eligibility, I urge the Government to consider pursuing two areas of improvement.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, we can organise existing schemes such that those with less severe forms of disability would still retain eligibility to some of the support schemes so that their needs can be better met.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the criteria for MediSave withdrawal for long-term care needs could be relaxed to allow those with mild disabilities to start withdrawing, while the other schemes continue to have a higher bar.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we can learn from existing schemes like MediFund and ComCare such that the level of financial support provided is tiered against the extent of care need, which, in this case, could be approximated by the extent of disability.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, CareShield Life payouts can start progressively when one is unable to complete one ADL independently, albeit with a smaller payout.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Failing to do so means that CareShield Life, in essence, acts as a severe disability insurance, rather than the intended long-term care insurance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to relieving some financial burden, receiving financial resources earlier in a graduated approach may also allow more Singaporeans to better access rehabilitation services that could reduce the worsening of their condition, or even prevent further conditions or disabilities from developing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, supporting these families at an earlier stage relieves caregiver stress and anxiety and allows them to focus on other aspects of life like work, parenting and more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: All of these are likely to create downstream cost-savings and, more importantly, enhance the well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that CareShield Life premiums are gender-differentiated due to actuarial assessments, but our society surely should not be defined by these numbers solely, just like how our other social and health policies are not defined along these lines.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Both men and women receive fair and equal treatment regardless of statistical differences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They receive the same amount of healthcare subsidies and benefits despite the greater susceptibility of women to chronic illness and disabilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This similar treatment for all, regardless of gender, should be continued in the payment of CareShield Life premiums, especially since the point of insurance, as we know, is to risk-pool.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Women may live longer than men, but they also live with less financial resources.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the same year, about four in 10 active CPF members who turned 55 in 2017 did not hit the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) of $83,000 in their Retirement Accounts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Among women, only 53% were able to reach the BRS, compared to 66% of men.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Every year, many more women than men drop out of the labour force to care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the 2018 Labour Force Survey, 75,000 women are outside the labour force to provide caregiving to relatives and families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, 80% of family caregivers who are outside the labour force are women.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They suffer from loss in income, affecting their ability to save for their own retirement and healthcare needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, when comparing with international practices, it is helpful to consider how the European Union's (EU's) highest court banned the practice by insurance companies of gender-differentiated premiums.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: An EU Court of Justice Grand Chamber case ruled that multiple EU legal instruments which mandate equal treatment between men and women do not allow for the use of sex as an actuarial factor in differentiating individuals’ premiums and benefits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Article 12 of our Constitution provides that "all persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has acknowledged in its latest Convention for Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) state report that the principle of equality for women is entrenched under this Article.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Surely then, women deserve equal protection and their premiums not be differentiated through actuarial factors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that designing a mandatory and national long-term care insurance scheme with a framework that discriminates based on gender will set us back a long way in pursuing gender equality.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must not forget the unaccounted value of how much women have contributed since the Independence of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of recognising and compensating the vastly unequal amount of unpaid work they do, it may appear that we are now proposing to further penalise them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this is not the kind of social compact we aspire to build.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our policies apply to those who are aged 30 and above.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand and appreciate the need for these schemes to support our ageing population, I must ask why do we discriminate against those who are aged below 30 because illnesses and disabilities can hit at any age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: CareShield Life covers pre-existing disabilities for all future cohorts, which is laudable.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But it leaves a huge gap for those who are severely disabled and require long-term care support before 30.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is even more so for children who are diagnosed with life-limiting diseases.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: My understanding from the ground is that these children and their families face immense long-term care costs, which include but are not limited to, hospitalisation, surgery, rehabilitation, special school, special transport, specific aids and machines, specialised milk powder and other consumables.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Other than CareShield Life, amendments to the CPF Act to allow MediSave withdrawals for long-term care should allow all to do so regardless of age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For children and youths who may not have CPF savings to tap on, we should also extend flexibility in allowing parents to tap on their MediSave accounts to support the long-term care needs for their children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand that we may want to ensure that parents themselves retain adequate CPF savings for their own retirement and healthcare needs, at the end of the day, the money must come from somewhere.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If it is not from their CPF MediSave account, it is likely that it has to be out of their own pockets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While we have good social safety nets, we must also consider that many of these schemes take into account the savings and assets possessed by the household.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As such, retirement adequacy and savings for healthcare costs in future will remain affected.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, allowing parents to tap on their CPF MediSave savings for their children is in line with our policy of family as the first line of support.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would also ensure consistency in policy, as current rules allow for parents to pay for the hospital bills of their children using their MediSave savings.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, it only provides $200 and, given the care needs and costs of our younger ones who may be equally ill or disabled, we ought to ensure that our other schemes support them adequately rather than discriminate against them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It would be sad for us to take good care of our seniors and forget about our younger generation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the lower prevalence of terminal illness and disability amongst our children and youths, we can afford to provide the same support we do for our seniors but at far less significant budget expansion and I hope that we will do the right thing and stand in solidarity with all Singaporeans regardless of age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The community practitioners who work with vulnerable seniors, differently-abled and low-income communities on the ground have spent countless hours trying to grasp the increasing complexity and fragmentation of our health, social and care systems and policies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Most of these schemes have an average of three eligibility criteria and these criteria differ across schemes in terms of age, extent of disability, household monthly income and more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these schemes require application through a social worker or directly to the relevant Government agency or alternatively require a disability assessment to be conducted.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: On the ground, awareness of these schemes is understandably an issue, and the concern will surely be for people who are severely disabled but may not have accessed touchpoints like hospitals or social service offices such that they could be directed to access this web of schemes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the support of these touchpoints, applications often take up significant portions of time for either care-recipients and/or their caregivers, as well as the social service or healthcare professional assigned to support them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The sheer number of schemes, accompanied by the number and variance in eligibility criteria and the amount of supporting documents required for the application, makes it overwhelming and exhausting for all involved.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the Silver Generation Office Ambassadors' work, limitations remain, especially in ensuring timely access to these schemes for those who desperately need support.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One of the cases that was shared with me is an elderly Singaporean male, let us call him Michael, who is married to a foreign spouse and resides in a 1-room rental flat.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Michael suffered from global aphasia and a stroke, and he was also diagnosed to suffer a permanent loss of mental capacity, ability to communicate and needed help in all ADLs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: When the volunteers met the family after Michael was discharged, they found that the family had insufficient money to put food on the table, and was also struggling to find money for transport to the hospital for the required medical care and proposed rehabilitation services.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can you wrap up in the next few seconds?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: It is clear that we need to urgently do more in providing care planning, navigation and coordination services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I believe that solidarity of all Singaporeans, regardless of age, gender or extent of disability, should be important guiding principles for a care system in a country which now ranks among the wealthiest in the world.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, in helping Singaporeans prepare for long-term care, the CareShield Life Bill that is being discussed today is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: People say that you have children to prepare for old age.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore today, just depending on our children for old age is not enough.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In future, as the population ages, preparing for old age will be increasingly challenging.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Last year, during the Parliamentary debate on the CareShield Life Committee Report, I said that the programme itself is self-sustaining but the implementation details need to be actively planned out.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, how do we assist those who cannot afford the premiums and include them in the programme so that no one is left behind?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What is the right direction for our social policies?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There is an ancient saying that in great harmony the aged are provided for till their end, the disabled are cared for, and people treat one another like their own kin.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: By pooling risks, we are able to pool resources together to assist the elderly and the disabled who are unable to care for themselves.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: By pooling risks, we can pay relatively low and affordable premiums to get comparatively high and meaningful payouts when needed.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The Bill today has provided a partial framework that is feasible and reasonable for our vision to care for the aged and disabled.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But aside from the Bill, the entire package should be carefully planned out.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If you have $600 in your pocket, do you have enough suitable options?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Are the fees affordable for those who require long-term care?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: None of us can anticipate when we could be hit by a sudden illness or sustain an injury that could affect our ability to go about essential daily activities and to work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we are not financially prepared, this will have serious impact on our life and our families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we would not wish for anyone to be severely disabled, we cannot predict when and who it will impact.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have a resident who, in his early 40s, suffered a stroke.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He was severely disabled as a result of the stroke.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Before the stroke, he was gainfully employed and the dual income that he and his wife made was more than sufficient to comfortably support his family and their three young children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Not only has the stroke rendered him unable to be work, he needs to be assisted in his daily living activities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: His wife’s single income is now supporting his ongoing care needs as well as their children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, financing his ongoing care needs as well as supporting their family's expenses have been and continues to be financially challenging for his wife and the children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have also had several residents who sought financial assistance for the long-term care needs of their parents who become severely disabled and need to stay in a nursing home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For middle-income families that do not qualify for Government subsidies, the cost is a few thousands monthly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have witnessed many families that are not financially prepared for such expenses and face difficulty in making these payments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If their parents had coverage for the disability similar to that of CareShield Life, the monthly payout would help alleviate some of the cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am supportive of the Bill to provide long-term care financing support for severely disabled persons, but I do have some clarifications and feedback on CareShield Life and Long-Term Care.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Those in this age group are in their 30s to 40s and are at the stage of their life when they have many responsibilities and financial demands.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, if they are married and have children, they would need to support their young families, pay the mortgages on their homes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They may also have to take care of an aged parent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As enrollment into CareShield Life is compulsory and not an option for this group, how can they be assured that CareShield Life premiums are fair and competitive as compared to premiums of other similar insurance covered by private entities?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the scheme being compulsory, the risk pool will be large and it would be expected that premiums will be affordable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What assurance is there for Singaporeans that premiums will be kept low and affordable?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As it has been stated that payouts will increase about 2% each year to adjust for the higher cost of long-term care in future, premiums will be expected to increase in tandem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, will the transitional subsidies and means-tested subsidies be sufficient to keep premiums affordable?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MOH assure them that for our people and these age groups that taking on long-term care coverage at a young age, that they would be better off than delaying that to a later time?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given that the various healthcare coverage plans and schemes that are already in place, more information should also be shared to show how CareShield Life complements and is not a duplication.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Feedback from the ground is that there are so many schemes and eligibility criteria for these schemes and understanding the various schemes and objectives can be quite confusing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While MediSave funds can be used to make payment for CareShield Life premiums, with the changing employment trends and disruption in jobs and employments, income contributions to MediSave may be affected.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may impact ability to make payout for CareShield Life and other premiums like MediShield Life and Integrated Shield Plans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, what are the implications if an individual loses his job and will his coverage lapse if he is unable to pay for his CareShield Life premiums?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What help, if any, can he get to assist him during this period when there is disruption?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Feedback, as we have heard from many other Members in this Chamber, is that the criterion for at least three ADLs may be somewhat strict.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But regardless, when one is already in the unfortunate position of being afflicted with disability, what help will there be to ensure that the process for disability assessment and eligibility will not be onerous?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For those with two ADLs on the CareShield Life scheme who do participate in the CareShield Life Scheme and they are not eligible for the claim payouts when they do get disabled, do they need to continue to pay future premiums for CareShield Life if they are unable to work or to continue to work?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will affect their ability to afford premiums in the future if they are already unable to do the two ADLs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could the Minister share how this group would be treated if they do have ADLs but are not able to qualify for the payouts?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am going to ask some operational and procedural or practical questions with regard to CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The reason why I am asking is that, during the briefings that I conducted with our Merdeka Generation (MG) seniors, it was quite interesting because many expressed interest to participate in CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They do, however, need to have more information to help them understand CareShield Life, most importantly, to assess if they can afford it and how to participate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some of the MG seniors I met – unfortunately, I have to say this – but many that I met were not sure whether they are on ElderShield or not, because they said "I do not know whether I opted in or whether I opted out".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, they do need some help to also check on that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do want to take the opportunity at this point to also give feedback because the information online with regard to CareShield Life has been actually quite comprehensive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, the Online Calculator for CareShield Life premiums is very easy to use and very simple.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The only problem is you need to have certain information, like whether you have ElderShield or not.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, for some of our seniors, they could answer all the other questions except that, so they could not estimate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think these are very practical but important matters that I hope more clarity can be provided to our seniors soon.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mental illness and dementia can significantly impair cognitive and behavioural functioning and interfere with normal activities and relationships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These can be as disabling as any other physical disabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Dementia and mental illnesses are sometimes called invisible disabilities and may impact an individual's ability to do essential daily activities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope that we can look at how mental illness and conditions like dementia could be treated or would be assessed together with the ADLs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Based on the report on "The Burden of Disease in Singapore between 1990 to 2017", Singapore faces a challenge shared by many developed countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While life expectancy has increased, the number of years that is spent in poor health has not decreased.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Lifestyle and habits increase the risk of disabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The leading risk factors affecting health in Singapore in 2017 were dietary risks, tobacco, high blood pressure and high blood sugar.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The leading causes of Years Lived with Disability (LYD) in Singapore were musculoskeletal disorders, mental disorders, unintentional injuries and neurological disorders.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, it is important that we leverage the data that we have on our healthcare trends, assess the risks together and also encourage regular health screening as I believe that this will help support early detection and enable appropriate and timely interventions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may help mitigate some of the risks of severe disability associated with chronic diseases and enable Singaporeans to live better quality lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can expect the centralisation of expertise in the management of the schemes to yield the benefits of economies of scale, consistency and reduce running costs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The schemes are intended to provide long-term care financing support for severely disabled persons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our rapidly ageing population and longer lifespans, many of our frail elderly will tap upon this assistance towards the end of their lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My concern is that some elderly and their families may not be aware of such assistance and do not know how to apply for help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to reach out to this group of vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would this result in the latter's MediSave being depleted, leaving them little for their own use when they themselves become older?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The department in charge must ensure that vulnerable Singaporeans know how to apply for assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another concern for me is that MediSave can be used to pay for long-term care for people with severe disabilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As life expectancies increase and family sizes shrink, would the younger generation's MediSave accounts be depleted such that they would not be able to tap into the funds in their own old age?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): I am also concerned about the security of personal data in MOH's electronic databases.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share an update on the measures to fortify protection of this information?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those commonly reported to be more effective than their generic cousins, please kindly review the demand for these drugs and consider subsidising them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has been enhancing policies and investing in resources to promote active, healthy living among Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This should help to prolong the duration of healthy years.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to thank the Health Promotion Board for bringing in all kinds of exercises – Zumba Gold, stretchband, yoga and so on – free of charge to our community, all the parks, pavilions and condominiums.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the process, they also improve their bonding.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have residents who go to exercise and later they arrange overseas trips together, such as one-day Batam trips, three-day Malacca trips and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, chronic health and mobility problems are inevitable for most who are in old age.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is important, therefore, for one to be self-sufficient.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially so when one is retired or unable to work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Looking at current global trends, more people are likely to stay single or choose not to have children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, relying on the younger generations for financial support is not always an option.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, those who have children would typically not wish to burden them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, we have CareShield Life to help Singaporeans to be self-sufficient with the support from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, it is not only the elderly who may find themselves with mobility impairment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Younger people, too, may require long-term care due to illness or accidents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is quite worrying because some within this group would be those who do not have ElderShield or any form of insurance coverage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are additional subsidies for Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation citizens.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I have spoken to older residents and they are unmoved by the subsidies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are retired or do not have a full-time job and the idea of having to commit a sum of money each month to an intangible concept is daunting to them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, many healthy, mobile people have the "it will never happen to me" mentality.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, they do not see the necessity of making a small investment to insure themselves against possible severe disability.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, there is a sizeable percentage of young people, adults included, who still do not understand how MediShield works.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And they would only call up CPF to ask for clarifications when they are hospitalised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, when one does not understand the full benefits of a scheme, they are far less likely to put faith and their money in it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have to go beyond subsidies to encourage a wider take-up rate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, the people who stand to benefit most from the scheme will be left out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, hopefully, the Ministry would have some education campaign to reach out to this group to explain the different schemes so that people fully understand the schemes and they can reap the benefits when they need them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   CareShield Life will look after people with disabilities.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, those born before 1970 will not be automatically enrolled and those born from 1970 to 1979 are only automatically enrolled under certain conditions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we encourage these people to join this scheme?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although there are additional subsidies for Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation citizens, however, many citizens told me that they are retired and there is no need to commit a sum of money each month to prevent something that is unlikely to happen.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They also do not know whether they will be eligible for claims even if they, indeed, develop some kind of disability.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to subsidies, I urge the Government to do more public education so that people know the benefits of this scheme and more Singaporeans will be protected.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Though I am aware that the topic of differential premium for men and women introduced for CareShield Life was widely debated previously, I would still like to state my stand and hope that MOH can review its position.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I do not agree that our society should go the route of differential premium by gender, causing gender divide.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, we may start the trend of potentially differentiating premiums in future by race or other genetic risk factors as we advance into precision medicine.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, as the Nominated Member representing the professional bodies in Singapore, I hope to bring awareness to the House, the Singapore Actuarial Society, a governance body for the actuarial profession in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Actuarial Society (SAS) was established in 1976.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Fellows of SAS are in most cases Fellows of the Society of Actuaries in the US, the Canadian Institute of Actuaries, Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (UK) or Institute of Actuaries of Australia.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Like other professional bodies, SAS requires Fellows to maintain and disclose annually a minimum level of continuing professional development.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The viability and sustainability of the CareShield Life Scheme are highly dependent on the appropriateness of the premiums and the adequacy of the assets in the CareShield Life and the ElderShield Fund to support the benefits promised under the scheme.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There may be uncertainties in how the experience will unfold and there is a lack of long-term care historical experience to guide an actuary in pricing and valuations.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To carry out the work, the consulting actuary has to transfer and adapt experience from other countries and draw up assumptions of future experience such that the likelihood of having to adjust the premiums is kept at an acceptable level, keeping in mind frequent adjustments to premiums leads to loss of confidence by the public in the scheme.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As the proposed Council member will be providing actuarial advice, a Fellow of SAS, who is governed by the standards and code of conduct of SAS, will be most appropriate for this role.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications and proposal above, I stand to support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will speak in favour of all these four aspects of the Bill successively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The not-for profit administration increases the affordability of premiums.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The centralisation of administering the scheme will streamline the application for payout process.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also allows for smoother transition for those who choose to shift from the ElderShield scheme to CareShield Life scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also allows for the funds to be combined into a single CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as the monies are consolidated into a single fund, how will the Minister ensure inter-generational equity in how the schemes are administered?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to the transition from ElderShield to CareShield Life, will the Minister provide an indication as to when and how sign-ups can begin?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, will Supplement Schemes for ElderShield be affected by the transfer of ElderShield to become Government-administered and change of coverage to CareShield Life instead of ElderShield should the policyholder choose to shift over to CareShield Life?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because healthcare can come in many forms, this flexibility is valuable for families to have yet another place of resources to tap into to care for the severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But even as there is increased flexibility, it should not deplete from MediSave funds to the extent that MediSave is no longer useful for its intended purpose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially acute where a child’s MediSave funds are used to pay for a parent's medical expenses, and the child has his or her own medical expenses to cover and, as a result of not marrying, the child does not have anyone else’s MediSave account to tap onto in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, the new section 16B(1)(a) of the Central Provident Fund Act found in clause 66 indicates that there is a minimum sum in the member’s account in order for cash withdrawals for long-term care to be allowed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, part 10 establishes the Long-Term Care Support Fund which is used for premium subsidies and other long-term care-related assistance as set out in clause 39.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister share with us what are some of the plans that the Ministry has in utilising the Funds for purposes other than subsidising CareShield Life premiums?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, what kind of assistance will there be for those who are severely disabled but have utilised the six years under the ElderShield scheme, those who were unable to purchase the ElderShield scheme because they had been severely disabled, and those who are low-income and do not have much in their MediSave account?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does the Minister seek to address these perceived gaps?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fourthly, this Bill introduces offences and penalties for the administration of this scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 49 criminalises the act of an assessor making a fraudulent disability assessment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the integrity of the administration of CareShield Life and ElderShield schemes rests primarily on the disability assessor, this offence places a safeguard against fraudulent claims facilitated by disability assessors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 50 criminalises the act of not applying the funds for the insured person first.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new section 16B(10) of the CPF Act also has a similar offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This offence ameliorates the risk of cash payouts being misused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the person directly harmed by the act criminalised by this offence is the insured person or member, why is it that a portion of the penalty be returned to the insured person himself or herself instead of having the whole penalty be paid into the CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the penalty is possibly more than the amount misused by four to eight times, requiring the offender to pay the insured person or member would not remove the punitive quality of the penalty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An exception to the offence is reasonable excuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because different households structure their expenses differently such that it may not be very clear whether the payout was used for the insured person or member first, would the Minister give some examples of what a reasonable excuse might be?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as this Bill seeks to provide some financial support for long-term care, financial support is only one side of the equation to ensuring that long-term care remains affordable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on the plans to ensure that we have sufficient personnel and facilities for this increase in demand?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because technology can help caring for severely disabled persons less physically demanding, how has Singapore been investing in such technology to reduce the reliance on foreign manpower and to allow those who work in this physically demanding field to enjoy a longer, meaningful career?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, what efforts have been made to make certain assistive technologies more accessible to families who may need it to care for their loved ones?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, however, we have, in broad terms, a good system in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Where the provision of fiscal measures to support a sustainable healthcare model is concerned, where good quality doctors are concerned, where professional and hardworking nursing population is concerned, I think Singapore ranks well and does well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I hope we can put things in perspective in this debate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But often, with long lives, though not necessarily so, come with it some loss of the kind of life as we knew it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Needing to rely on others to carry out ADLs does not just affect the elderly but also affects people from all ages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By setting up the Long-Term Care Support Fund, there can be more support for those who need more help in financing long-term care options, whether it be through subsidising premiums or through other schemes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because this Bill implements and commits to the caring of those who are severely disabled, and for the reasons I have stated, I support it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I have spoken on the importance of CareShield Life in 2018.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, I renew my support for it and I am glad that this Bill does not focus solely on CareShield Life but long-term care as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: CareShield Life has to be viewed within the frame of Singapore's long-term care plan.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government invested significant amounts of resources and effort to build up our system, policies and infrastructure to cope with the needs of a rapidly ageing population, strengthening them as we progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Government spending has also increased by multiple folds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Public healthcare expenditure, for instance, more than doubled in the past six years, and will continue to increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How we can sustain this is serious business.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ageing is a multifaceted issue covering physical, financial, psychological and social aspects of our lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given the growing silver population and longer lifespan, it is imperative that we have in place a comprehensive and effective long-term care system for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, we need a good ecosystem to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government cannot monopolise the care for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We will need community partners and Singaporeans, too, to address the challenges and needs of an ageing Singapore successfully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We will also need to plan early and act pre-emptively.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of the challenges faced in our old age may have their roots in our younger days.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Likewise, what we do right in our youth can also offer ourselves better protection when we become old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One such instance is insuring ourselves against calamities, such as severe disabilities in our old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, one in two healthy Singapore residents aged 65 could become severely disabled in their lifetime, not that rare after all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are not insignificant numbers, especially since severe disabilities can seriously strain one's psychological, physical and financial well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, similar to the philosophy underpinning MediShield Life, it is important that we consider and support CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through a public insurance, such as CareShield Life, we pool our risks and money to help fellow Singaporeans in need, sustainably.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are a society that believes in compassion and inclusivity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Schemes, like CareShield Life, translate such beliefs into real actions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite the clear imperative for CareShield Life, it is, nonetheless, a very complex scheme to understand, even for younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Different age groups start in different years and, even within the same cohort, there can be subgroups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, there are those who enrol in CareShield Life and those who remain in ElderShield.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If one thought MediShield Life was complex, CareShield Life topped it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, effective communications to address the "why" and "how" are critical to a successful implementation of CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the first part, I would like to talk about the "why" – persuading the young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite the high probability, our young today question the need for the scheme to be made mandatory for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many, who are still in the prime of health, do not anticipate severe disabilities when they age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many also do not see the urgency in planning for the possibility of age-related disabilities at this point.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, they want to preserve their autonomy in choosing whether and when to enrol themselves in a universal public insurance scheme.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, the sense of importance for risk pooling is diminished when they observe that the total claim of $100 million is only a small fraction of the total premium collection of $2.6 billion as at end 2015. "What happens to the huge sum of money remaining in the pool?", they ask. "Who pockets the rest?", the more cynical amongst them may also ask.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be fair, these concerns were answered before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps, people missed it and the message bears repeating.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I think it is also because there are too few stories of "success" in the case of ElderShield and too many stories of difficult claims that breed scepticism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hopefully, with CareShield Life to be managed fully by the Singapore Government, Singaporeans' confidence in the scheme will be boosted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Interesting to note, private life insurance hardly needs persuasion, despite events qualifying for claims being relatively rare.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As at 2018, life insurance sales grew at 7%.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, the total claim amount due to deaths and disabilities in 2018 was about 0.1% of the total sum insured.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is strong awareness of the need for life insurance, and credit goes to the army of insurance agents who actively educate the population on the ground face-to-face, a point worth pondering.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Women policyholders are expected to pay a higher premium than men.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The main reason articulated was that women have a longer lifespan on average and risks being disabled for a longer period of time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Arguably, however, the idea of a public insurance plan is to pool risks and resources to help one another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thus, should women not be allowed to pay the same amount of premium as the men in their respective cohorts?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many sacrificed their prime years to stay home and care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The years away from work mean they may have little or significantly less savings in their MediSave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These women may also not come from well-to-do families, who have little to contribute to their MediSave even if they wish to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is also no guarantee that their spouse or children, if they have any, will pay for their extra premiums.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How then do we ensure fairness and equity in the system?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For women who may have lost out to their male peers at work or who have made financial sacrifices for their families, what help can they look to receive?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, I would like to talk about communicating the "how" – "customer" experience.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: CareShield Life will see different years of commencement and impact on different age groups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Premium payments also differ across age groups and possibly within cohorts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These different ways of "slicing" ensure as many people are covered as possible, but it can be highly confusing, and soliciting buy-in will also be much harder.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, again, well-planned and targeted communications are imperative to a successful implementation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If the scheme cannot be simplified, the claim experience must certainly be simplified, and it must not disappoint.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A straightforward claim process comprising a one-stop solution without the need to approach different agencies for different documents will be useful and avoid the accusation of CareShield Life being a sinister plan that takes money from the people without the sincerity of giving back when needed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More importantly, when a person is already severely disabled, he or she cannot withstand complex processes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Overall, we could benefit from communicating how our Long-Term Care works in Singapore better and clearer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This Bill specifically covers the establishment of the Long-Term Care Support Fund.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is useful but we know Long-Term Care is more than just a fund.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we improve the Long-Term Care system over the years, we have been making announcements in piecemeal fashion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is understandable as we communicate whenever a new initiative becomes available.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the general public may not remember every initiative and consciously piece everything together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, may I humbly suggest the Government consider the following.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This could be done in schools as part of national education, through common touchpoints in the course of our lives and, of course, the usual mass media.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, high-touch method of engaging target groups when implementing and communicating complex schemes, such as CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, akin to how insurance agents make complex insurance schemes easy to understand, could there be a network of trained policy agents who would reach out to Singaporeans at the workplace or at home to explain complex schemes to them?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even the most well-meaning policies can fail if we fail to help Singaporeans understand and solicit their support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should also explore prevention and ways to minimise the risk.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a 2015 report by the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, it stated that there is a growing body of research literature underscoring the importance of fostering good health and habits in life to prevent or postpone the onset of morbidity at older ages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This should apply to age-related disabilities as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we must continue our efforts in encouraging healthier lifestyles and to do so from young.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Next, if I may please continue in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, in 2014, we had a vigorous debate on MediShield Life in Parliament and passed the Bill.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The purpose of passing that Bill was to provide universal healthcare insurance coverage so that all Singaporeans can enjoy basic healthcare protection.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Besides Government subsidies and our own MediSave savings, MediShield Life can help us cope with unforeseeable circumstances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The concept behind it is risk-pooling whereby everyone’s money is pooled together to allow people in need to pay for massive medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In principle and theory, CareShield Life and MediShield Life are the same.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is inevitable that Singaporeans must support one another through thick and thin.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the implementation of MediShield Life and CareShield Life is to prepare people not just for their own but others' future as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am sure we are all clear about the importance of CareShield Life after last year's and today's debate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my view, the key to the successful implementation of CareShield Life lies upon whether the Government can communicate it well, how it can explain the scheme in a targeted manner and address queries from different groups.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When MediShield was introduced, many people felt that it was a very complex policy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In truth, CareShield Life is even more complicated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, if people do not understand, they would not support it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If they do not support it, unhappiness may occur.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I hope that while we promote CareShield Life, we must also focus on communication and engage the people wholeheartedly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And this should not be limited to CareShield Life alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must let Singaporeans, young and old, to understand the concepts and methods of our eldercare system within the overall picture of the long-term care framework.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, we can, through civic education or ways that do not require exams, allow Singapore students to understand how we cope with the challenges of ageing and how we care for the aged, so that they are prepared at a young age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through such face-to-face in-depth explanations, I believe Singaporeans will be able to understand those important but not necessarily popular policies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Frankly speaking, the Government has taken a great deal of pain to look after the elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past, the Government has introduced many eldercare schemes and programmes, including CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Earlier on, the esteemed Member Mr Chen Show Mao mentioned that the care given under CareShield Life is not enough and that $600 can only pay for part of the expenses of the severely disabled.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am curious to learn from Mr Chen in what way can the Government do better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On a macro level, we have many different packages and subsides, I would like to know from Mr Chen what are the areas that we can improve on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, there are many suggestions raised in Parliament, not just from Mr Chen, for the Government to consider.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, when we raise these suggestions, we must be aware that, after all, someone will have to pay for it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government needs to allocate precious resources to the things we ask for, and it must balance different interests and tradeoffs to formulate the best possible policies to help Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The efforts that the Government has made is not simple at all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, when we are looking at issues pertaining to long-term care and ageing, we tend to be a bit passive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should adopt more proactive measures, such as encouraging Singaporeans to pay attention to their diet when they are young, stay fit, so that they can have a healthy foundation as they grow old and be able to enjoy a happy retirement life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My sincere hope is that we will all enjoy good health, lead a full and fulfilling life, and rather than having to spend on our care needs, are able to spend on things that we enjoy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we can never be sure of what will happen to us in the years to come.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It would be too late if we only start to worry or find ways to finance our care needs later in life when our familial obligations intensify, or worse, when we suffer disabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also unsustainable and unfortunate if we have to burden future generations – which is by the way shrinking because of our ageing population – to fund our own care needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This does not mean that the Government can cut back its support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This does not exonerate individuals from exercising personal responsibility, but this does enable us to pool our risks and help our fellow countrymen through times of need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a society that expounds the importance of compassion and inclusion, all of us will need to contribute, in ways big or small, in one way or another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will round up this debate on behalf of Minister Gan Kim Yong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Minister Gan has outlined, Singaporeans are living longer and healthier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, many of us will face the risk of severe disability and require long-term care at some point in our lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, it is important that we protect ourselves and our families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have been rolling out services to support Singaporeans in old age and we have more than doubled in this respect the home care and day-care places since 2011.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continuously look at key aspects of ageing and also the related issues around successful and active ageing, including, as Mr Leon Perera has exhorted, the use of technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will anchor the response around the key principles of inclusiveness, affordability and sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An inclusive long-term care financing system is one that supports all Singaporeans and enables them to afford essential basic long-term care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The design architecture of the Scheme must be to achieve that goal – to support Singaporeans and be able to do so while keeping premiums affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such a design is essential to protect vulnerable groups, such as the lower income and those with pre-existing disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many have previously decided to opt out from ElderShield, or may have made other long-term care financing arrangements of their own.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the older cohorts would also have fewer economically active years left to spread out their premiums, and hence face higher entry premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Given that the Scheme remains optional for these cohorts, members of these cohorts will need to assess their own preparations, their own provisions for long-term care, when deciding whether or not to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To address Dr Chia Shi-Lu's point, we will provide ample Government support and incentives to encourage their participation in CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would also like to assure Mr Png Eng Huat that those who are not severely disabled in existing cohorts can still join CareShield Life when it is launched in 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Png also sought clarifications on clause 6(4).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This clause is used to cater for exceptional situations, such as when someone had submitted an application for CareShield Life and it is being processed but, in the interim, fell into disability before the Scheme was effected or valid for this person.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This clause allows the Minister to use flexibility to still provide CareShield Life cover on compassionate grounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it is used in those limited exceptional circumstances and certainly not to be used arbitrarily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As CareShield Life remains optional for existing cohorts, we will not be able to cover those in the existing cohorts who are already severely disabled, and I think Mr Png Eng Huat understands this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan had raised this as well and I also hope that this addresses the point because if you cover everyone who is already severely disabled, that has an immediate impact on the premium that has to be borne by the remaining persons who subscribed onto the Scheme at that stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These individuals with pre-existing severe disabilities will be able to make claims immediately under the Scheme and so it is going to impact on the way in which you price the premiums for the rest of the members and also have an impact on whether their peers decide to join the Scheme or not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not a sustainable insurance scheme design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, we will assist these Singaporeans with pre-existing disability in other ways and I will elaborate on them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Christopher de Souza asked how ElderShield and ElderShield Supplement coverage will be affected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
